screens.title: What is System Design and Why Does It Matter?
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson we treat system design as the craft of turning user needs into concrete blueprints that engineers build. Think of an architect designing a skyscraper: they plan both what the building must do and how it will remain safe, powered, and accessible at scale. In software, that means deciding on storage, communication patterns, service decomposition, and non-functional requirements like reliability and performance. Good design prevents systems from becoming slow, costly, or fragile. Poor design creates outages, data loss, and technical debt. You will learn to identify the core attributes of well-designed systems—scalability, reliability, performance, and maintainability—and understand how distributed components like databases, caches, and queues interact to support real user traffic. This chapter also explains why system design is central to senior interviews: it tests your ability to reason about trade-offs, communicate architecture clearly, and design for ambiguity. By the end you will be able to break a product into functional pieces, call out key non-functional needs, and sketch a resilient, scalable solution. To get started, notice three key topics we will explore: defining system design, understanding distributed systems, and mapping non-functional requirements to concrete components.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: System design is both art and engineering: it aligns functional features with non-functional guarantees to deliver scalable, reliable systems.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › What is System Design
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
What is System Design and Why It Matters
Learn how architects of software translate requirements into resilient, scalable blueprints and why that skill is essential for senior engineers and system design interviews.
In this lesson
Define system design, map functional and non-functional needs, and see how components like caches and queues support scale.
Why it matters
A solid design reduces outages, lowers cost, and enables teams to evolve a product without crippling refactors.
Explore Key Topics
System Design
Architecture, components, and interfaces that meet both functional and non-functional needs.
Distributed Systems
How multiple services communicate and coordinate to serve large-scale users.
Non-functional Requirements
Performance, reliability, and maintainability that determine operational success.
Concept Map
Core elements: users and features, system components, operational guarantees.
Quick tip
When sketching a system, always name the critical non-functional needs first — they drive component choice and topology.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this first objective set we define the core skills you will acquire. First, you will be able to define system design as a multidisciplinary practice that spans architecture, components, interfaces, and data. Defining the term matters because it frames how you approach problems: you shift from line-by-line coding to planning for scale and resilience. Second, you will explain why system design is critical for building scalable, reliable, and maintainable systems. This includes describing concrete non-functional requirements and how they shape component choices. Third, you'll understand why system design is a core assessment in senior interviews: interviewers look for trade-off reasoning, clear communication, and practical experience building systems. Finally, you will identify the attributes of a well-designed system — scalability, reliability, performance, and maintainability — and explain how they influence design decisions. Each objective pairs a definition with a practice: for example, when you state a non-functional requirement like low latency, you will also suggest components such as caches or CDNs that address it. These skills prepare you to approach ambiguous, large-scale problems with structure and clarity.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice and Application
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide emphasizes applying the skills in practical settings. You will practice translating user stories into component-level sketches, listing both functional features and non-functional constraints. For example, if the requirement is video streaming to millions of users, you will list streaming, search, and personalization as core functions, and low latency and global availability as critical non-functional needs. You will also learn to propose candidate components — such as CDNs for distribution, caches for hot data, and message queues for asynchronous work — and justify those choices by referencing the non-functional requirements. Another objective is recognizing common pitfalls: prioritizing rapid development without planning for scale creates technical debt and single points of failure. Finally, you will practice evaluation: given a proposed architecture, you will reason about its scalability and reliability, and suggest targeted improvements. These applied skills mirror what senior interviews assess — clarity of thought, practical trade-offs, and the ability to evolve a design under constraints.

screens.title: Defining System Design
screens.narratorSegment: System design is the structured process of defining a system's architecture, components, modules, interfaces, and data to meet specified requirements. This definition matters because it changes the questions you ask: instead of only implementing a feature, you consider how that feature will operate under load, how it fails, and how it evolves. A concrete example: building a search feature requires not only index and query logic but also storage choices for the index, cache strategies for hot queries, and a plan for global distribution if users are worldwide. A common misconception is to treat system design as purely diagramming boxes and arrows. In reality, good design is multidisciplinary: it integrates software engineering, network behavior, operational concerns, and business constraints. To ground this idea, use a layered card display: one card defines the term, a second lists responsibilities (components, interfaces, NFRs), a third gives the skyscraper analogy, and a fourth offers a short example like a streaming service. Key takeaway: defining system design early surfaces critical trade-offs and guides component selection. Question to reflect on: When you name a component, which non-functional requirement motivated it?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: System design describes architecture and operational constraints so teams can build systems that meet both functional and non-functional goals.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Defining System Design
Definition
What the discipline covers
System design defines architecture, components, interfaces, and data so a team can implement a system that meets both functional and operational needs.
Responsibilities
  • Choose storage and data models that support scale.
  • Define communication and failure-recovery patterns.
  • Specify operational metrics and SLAs tied to business needs.
Analogy & Example
Skyscraper analogy
Architects plan function, structure, power, and flow. Similarly, system designers plan features, reliability, capacity, and evolution. Example: video streaming needs content storage, CDN, encoding, and user session handling.
Key Takeaway
A clear definition aligns teams and surfaces trade-offs before implementation begins.

screens.title: Monolithic vs Distributed Systems
screens.narratorSegment: Modern systems are rarely single-process monoliths; they typically become distributed collections of services, databases, caches, and queues. A monolith bundles functionality into one deployable unit. Its advantages include simplicity of deployment and fewer network boundaries, which can accelerate early development. But a common problem emerges as load grows: a single server becomes a single point of failure and scaling vertically is costly and limited. Distributed systems split functionality across services and machines, enabling horizontal scaling and redundancy. For example, an e-commerce site might separate user authentication, catalog search, and order processing into distinct services with their own databases and caches. This separation improves scalability and fault isolation, but introduces new concerns: network latency, partial failures, data consistency, and operational complexity. A frequent misconception is that distribution always improves performance; in fact, adding network hops can increase latency unless design choices like caching and data partitioning are applied. Key takeaway: choose the architecture that matches growth and operational capacity. Reflect: which parts of an application should you separate first to reduce risk without exploding complexity? Monolithic vs Distributed Systems means monoliths simplify early work; distributed systems provide scale and resilience at the cost of network complexity and operational overhead.. In practical terms, understanding the shift and the trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Monoliths simplify early work; distributed systems provide scale and resilience at the cost of network complexity and operational overhead.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Monolithic vs Distributed
Monolithic
Single deployable unit
  • Simple local calls, fast early development.
  • Challenges: vertical scaling limits, single point of failure.
  • Risk of tangled code and costly refactors.
Common mistake
Assuming a monolith will scale indefinitely without redesign.
Distributed
Multiple services across networked machines
  • Enables horizontal scaling and fault isolation.
  • Requires handling network failures, latency, and consistency.
  • Often involves databases, caches, message queues, and CDNs.
Pro tip
Extract services that reduce operational risk first: user auth, billing, and order processing are common early candidates.

screens.title: Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements
screens.narratorSegment: A core step in system design is distinguishing functional requirements — what the system must do — from non-functional requirements — how the system must behave. Functional requirements are feature-driven: for a video platform, streaming, search, and profile management are examples. Non-functional requirements, often abbreviated as NFRs, include performance, scalability, reliability, and security. These NFRs often dictate architecture: a requirement for low latency suggests caches or edge CDNs; a need for high availability leads to redundancy across zones. An important misconception is to treat NFRs as secondary; in practice they are primary constraints that shape component choice and topology. Use a short process: 1) gather functional features, 2) list NFRs and rank them, 3) map components that satisfy top NFRs, 4) validate trade-offs. Concrete example: if low latency and global reach are top NFRs for streaming, you choose global CDNs, edge caching, and regional storage rather than a single central data center. Key takeaway: always state the dominant NFRs before designing topologies. Reflecting question: which NFR would you prioritize for a financial transaction service and why? Functional vs Non-Functional Requirements means non-functional requirements are the primary drivers for architectural choices; state them early and use them to justify components.. In practical terms, how both guide design decisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Functional
Features the system provides
  • Examples: stream video, search catalog, manage profiles.
  • Drive APIs and data models.
  • Often stable but evolve with product needs.
Non-functional
Operational guarantees
  • Examples: latency, throughput, availability, security.
  • These constraints determine cache, replication, and partitioning choices.

screens.title: Core Components: Databases, Caches, Queues, CDNs
screens.narratorSegment: System design repeatedly uses a modest set of components to meet requirements. Databases store durable data and choose trade-offs between consistency and scale. Caches reduce latency and offload read traffic from primary stores; they are essential when low latency is a priority. Message queues decouple producers and consumers, allowing asynchronous work and smoothing traffic spikes. CDNs push content closer to users to reduce latency and bandwidth costs. A concrete example: a video streaming service uses object storage for raw files, a CDN to serve playback to users worldwide, a metadata database for catalog data, and a cache for hot recommendations. A common misconception is to overuse caches without invalidation strategy; stale caches cause correctness issues. When choosing components, map them to specific NFRs: need low latency? Use caches and CDNs. Need durability and transactions? Choose databases with the appropriate consistency model. Key takeaway: components are tools, and the right selection follows from stated non-functional needs and the anticipated load patterns. Core Components: Databases, Caches, Queues, CDNs means select components by the non-functional needs they satisfy: caches for latency, cdns for global reach, queues for decoupling.. In practical terms, common building blocks and why each exists. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Component mapping
keyIdea.text: Select components by the non-functional needs they satisfy: caches for latency, CDNs for global reach, queues for decoupling.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Core Components
Database
Durable state and queries
Choose based on consistency, query patterns, and scale. Relational for transactions; NoSQL for flexible schemas and high write rates.
Cache
Fast reads and latency reduction
Caches reduce database load but require invalidation strategies to avoid stale data problems.
Queue
Decoupling and asynchrony
Queues buffer spikes and allow background processing for tasks like notifications or batch jobs.
CDN
Global content delivery
A CDN caches static or streamable assets near users to lower latency and bandwidth costs.
Example
Streaming service: object storage for files, CDN for playback, metadata DB for catalog, cache for hot queries, queue for transcoding jobs.

screens.title: Scalability: What It Means and How to Achieve It
screens.narratorSegment: Scalability is the system's ability to handle increasing load by adding resources. It can be vertical (bigger machines) or horizontal (more machines). Vertical scaling is easy to reason about but hits physical and cost limits. Horizontal scaling requires designing for statelessness where possible, partitioning data, and using replication and sharding strategies. A concrete example: an A P I serving user requests can be made stateless so multiple instances behind a load balancer share traffic; stateful components like user sessions or databases need partitioning or sticky approaches. Common mistakes include scaling only the application layer while leaving the database as a bottleneck, or neglecting data partitioning until performance degrades. Practical strategies: introduce caches for read-heavy workloads, shard data by a stable key for write scale, and add read replicas for scaled reads. Key takeaway: plan for scaling early by identifying the likely bottlenecks—compute, storage, or network—and align your topology to distribute load across those resources. Reflect: which part of your application is most likely to become a scaling bottleneck and why? Scalability: What It Means and How to Achieve It means design for horizontal scale by making services stateless, partitioning state, and aligning components to workload patterns.. In practical terms, strategies for handling growth without collapse. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Scalability
What is scalability?
Ability to handle growth by adding resources. Vertical scale increases power of a node; horizontal scale adds more nodes.
Make services stateless where possible.
Shard data by stable keys to spread writes.
Use read replicas and caches for read-heavy workloads.
Common mistake
Assuming adding servers fixes all bottlenecks without addressing shared state like databases.
Example
An API becomes stateless, runs multiple instances behind a load balancer, uses Redis to cache hot lookups, and shards user data by user ID to support write scale.
Key Takeaway
Identify bottlenecks early and match scaling strategy to the specific resource under pressure.

screens.title: Reliability and Fault Tolerance
screens.narratorSegment: Reliability is the probability a system performs its intended function without failure over time. Fault tolerance is the design practice that allows systems to continue operating despite component failures. Practical approaches include redundancy, health checks and automatic failover, graceful degradation, and retry patterns with backoff. For example, a user-facing service should detect a downstream database failure and fall back to a read-only mode, serving cached content instead of failing completely. A common misconception is that adding retries solves transient failures; without exponential backoff and idempotency, retries can worsen cascading failures under load. When designing for reliability, quantify acceptable downtime and recovery time objectives, then apply patterns like replication, leader election, and circuit breakers to meet those targets. Key takeaway: reliability is engineered through redundancy and careful handling of partial failures; design early for observable failure modes and clear recovery strategies. Reflect: which failure scenarios can you tolerate and which require automated recovery? Reliability and Fault Tolerance means design for partial failures with redundancy, graceful degradation, and controlled retries to keep users safe during incidents.. In practical terms, ensuring the system continues to operate under failure. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Reliability
Core idea
Reliability is the chance a system keeps working over time; fault tolerance keeps parts failing without total outage.
Redundancy and replication
Graceful degradation and fallbacks
Circuit breakers and backoff for retries
Common misconception
Blind retries without backoff can amplify failures and increase downtime.
Scenario
If a primary database becomes slow, failover to replicas for reads, queue writes for replay, and use cached data to preserve user experience.
Key Takeaway
Plan for realistic failures: detect, isolate, and recover with minimal user impact.

screens.title: Performance: Latency and Throughput
screens.narratorSegment: Performance in system design refers to two related ideas: latency — how quickly a system responds to a request — and throughput — how many requests it can handle per unit time. Both matter, but they drive different tactics. To lower latency, you may add caches, optimize critical code paths, or use CDNs for static content. To increase throughput, you may replicate stateless servers, partition data, or parallelize processing. A concrete example: a search A P I needs low latency to feel snappy, so you cache popular queries and precompute indices. However, during peak indexing, throughput matters for how fast you can process new documents; here you might queue indexing jobs and scale consumers horizontally. A common pitfall is optimizing for average latency while ignoring tail latency; long outliers cause poor user experience even if averages look good. Key takeaway: measure both latency and throughput, prioritize the metrics tied to user experience, and choose remedies that match the measurement. Reflect: which metric most directly influences your user's perception in your chosen app? narration.text: Performance in system design refers to two related ideas: latency — how quickly a system responds to a request — and throughput — how many requests it can handle per unit time. Both matter, but they drive different tactics. To lower latency, you may add caches, optimize critical code paths, or use CDNs for static content. A concrete example: a search A P I needs low latency to feel snappy, so you cache popular queries and precompute indices. A common pitfall is optimizing for average latency while ignoring tail latency; long outliers cause poor user experience even if averages look good. screens.title: Maintainability and Technical Debt
screens.narratorSegment: Maintainability is the ease with which a system can be understood, modified, and repaired. Poor design choices early lead to technical debt: shortcuts that incur future cost. Examples include tightly coupled modules, unclear interfaces, or lack of automated tests. screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Let's review six core concepts to carry forward. First, system design: it defines architecture, components, interfaces, and data aligned to requirements. Second, distributed systems: most modern applications are composed of networked components that must coordinate across machines. Third, scalability: design choices like stateless services, caching, and sharding enable growth. Fourth, reliability: redundancy, graceful degradation, and controlled retries keep systems running under failure. Fifth, performance: latency and throughput are distinct metrics that require different remedies. Sixth, non-functional requirements: these operational constraints drive component selection and topology. A useful habit is to name the dominant NFRs at the start of any design exercise — they will focus your choices and make trade-offs explicit. Closing reflection: which of these concepts do you find easiest to reason about, and which will you practice next?

fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this lesson we treat system design as the craft of turning user needs into concrete blueprints that engineers build. Think of an architect designing a skyscraper: they plan both what the building must do and how it will remain safe, powered, and accessible at scale. In software, that means deciding on storage, communication patterns, service decomposition, and non-functional requirements like reliability and performance. Good design prevents systems from becoming slow, costly, or fragile. Poor design creates outages, data loss, and technical debt. You will learn to identify the core attributes of well-designed systems—scalability, reliability, performance, and maintainability—and understand how distributed components like databases, caches, and queues interact to support real user traffic. This chapter also explains why system design is central to senior interviews: it tests your ability to reason about trade-offs, communicate architecture clearly, and design for ambiguity. By the end you will be able to break a product into functional pieces, call out key non-functional needs, and sketch a resilient, scalable solution. To get started, notice three key topics we will explore: defining system design, understanding distributed systems, and mapping non-functional requirements to concrete components.

In this first objective set we define the core skills you will acquire. First, you will be able to define system design as a multidisciplinary practice that spans architecture, components, interfaces, and data. Defining the term matters because it frames how you approach problems: you shift from line-by-line coding to planning for scale and resilience. Second, you will explain why system design is critical for building scalable, reliable, and maintainable systems. This includes describing concrete non-functional requirements and how they shape component choices. Third, you'll understand why system design is a core assessment in senior interviews: interviewers look for trade-off reasoning, clear communication, and practical experience building systems. Finally, you will identify the attributes of a well-designed system — scalability, reliability, performance, and maintainability — and explain how they influence design decisions. Each objective pairs a definition with a practice: for example, when you state a non-functional requirement like low latency, you will also suggest components such as caches or CDNs that address it. These skills prepare you to approach ambiguous, large-scale problems with structure and clarity.

This second objectives slide emphasizes applying the skills in practical settings. You will practice translating user stories into component-level sketches, listing both functional features and non-functional constraints. For example, if the requirement is video streaming to millions of users, you will list streaming, search, and personalization as core functions, and low latency and global availability as critical non-functional needs. You will also learn to propose candidate components — such as CDNs for distribution, caches for hot data, and message queues for asynchronous work — and justify those choices by referencing the non-functional requirements. Another objective is recognizing common pitfalls: prioritizing rapid development without planning for scale creates technical debt and single points of failure. Finally, you will practice evaluation: given a proposed architecture, you will reason about its scalability and reliability, and suggest targeted improvements. These applied skills mirror what senior interviews assess — clarity of thought, practical trade-offs, and the ability to evolve a design under constraints.

System design is the structured process of defining a system's architecture, components, modules, interfaces, and data to meet specified requirements. This definition matters because it changes the questions you ask: instead of only implementing a feature, you consider how that feature will operate under load, how it fails, and how it evolves. A concrete example: building a search feature requires not only index and query logic but also storage choices for the index, cache strategies for hot queries, and a plan for global distribution if users are worldwide. A common misconception is to treat system design as purely diagramming boxes and arrows. In reality, good design is multidisciplinary: it integrates software engineering, network behavior, operational concerns, and business constraints. To ground this idea, use a layered card display: one card defines the term, a second lists responsibilities (components, interfaces, NFRs), a third gives the skyscraper analogy, and a fourth offers a short example like a streaming service. Key takeaway: defining system design early surfaces critical trade-offs and guides component selection. Question to reflect on: When you name a component, which non-functional requirement motivated it?

Modern systems are rarely single-process monoliths; they typically become distributed collections of services, databases, caches, and queues. A monolith bundles functionality into one deployable unit. Its advantages include simplicity of deployment and fewer network boundaries, which can accelerate early development. But a common problem emerges as load grows: a single server becomes a single point of failure and scaling vertically is costly and limited. Distributed systems split functionality across services and machines, enabling horizontal scaling and redundancy. For example, an e-commerce site might separate user authentication, catalog search, and order processing into distinct services with their own databases and caches. This separation improves scalability and fault isolation, but introduces new concerns: network latency, partial failures, data consistency, and operational complexity. A frequent misconception is that distribution always improves performance; in fact, adding network hops can increase latency unless design choices like caching and data partitioning are applied. Key takeaway: choose the architecture that matches growth and operational capacity. Reflect: which parts of an application should you separate first to reduce risk without exploding complexity? Monolithic vs Distributed Systems means monoliths simplify early work; distributed systems provide scale and resilience at the cost of network complexity and operational overhead.. In practical terms, understanding the shift and the trade-offs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A core step in system design is distinguishing functional requirements — what the system must do — from non-functional requirements — how the system must behave. Functional requirements are feature-driven: for a video platform, streaming, search, and profile management are examples. Non-functional requirements, often abbreviated as NFRs, include performance, scalability, reliability, and security. These NFRs often dictate architecture: a requirement for low latency suggests caches or edge CDNs; a need for high availability leads to redundancy across zones. An important misconception is to treat NFRs as secondary; in practice they are primary constraints that shape component choice and topology. Use a short process: 1) gather functional features, 2) list NFRs and rank them, 3) map components that satisfy top NFRs, 4) validate trade-offs. Concrete example: if low latency and global reach are top NFRs for streaming, you choose global CDNs, edge caching, and regional storage rather than a single central data center. Key takeaway: always state the dominant NFRs before designing topologies. Reflecting question: which NFR would you prioritize for a financial transaction service and why? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

System design repeatedly uses a modest set of components to meet requirements. Databases store durable data and choose trade-offs between consistency and scale. Caches reduce latency and offload read traffic from primary stores; they are essential when low latency is a priority. Message queues decouple producers and consumers, allowing asynchronous work and smoothing traffic spikes. CDNs push content closer to users to reduce latency and bandwidth costs. A concrete example: a video streaming service uses object storage for raw files, a CDN to serve playback to users worldwide, a metadata database for catalog data, and a cache for hot recommendations. A common misconception is to overuse caches without invalidation strategy; stale caches cause correctness issues. When choosing components, map them to specific NFRs: need low latency? Use caches and CDNs. Need durability and transactions? Choose databases with the appropriate consistency model. Key takeaway: components are tools, and the right selection follows from stated non-functional needs and the anticipated load patterns. Scalability is the system's ability to handle increasing load by adding resources. It can be vertical (bigger machines) or horizontal (more machines). Vertical scaling is easy to reason about but hits physical and cost limits. Horizontal scaling requires designing for statelessness where possible, partitioning data, and using replication and sharding strategies. A concrete example: an A P I serving user requests can be made stateless so multiple instances behind a load balancer share traffic; stateful components like user sessions or databases need partitioning or sticky approaches. Common mistakes include scaling only the application layer while leaving the database as a bottleneck, or neglecting data partitioning until performance degrades. Practical strategies: introduce caches for read-heavy workloads, shard data by a stable key for write scale, and add read replicas for scaled reads. Key takeaway: plan for scaling early by identifying the likely bottlenecks—compute, storage, or network—and align your topology to distribute load across those resources. Reflect: which part of your application is most likely to become a scaling bottleneck and why? Reliability is the probability a system performs its intended function without failure over time. Fault tolerance is the design practice that allows systems to continue operating despite component failures. Let's review six core concepts to carry forward. First, system design: it defines architecture, components, interfaces, and data aligned to requirements. Second, distributed systems: most modern applications are composed of networked components that must coordinate across machines. Third, scalability: design choices like stateless services, caching, and sharding enable growth. Fourth, reliability: redundancy, graceful degradation, and controlled retries keep systems running under failure. Fifth, performance: latency and throughput are distinct metrics that require different remedies. Sixth, non-functional requirements: these operational constraints drive component selection and topology. A useful habit is to name the dominant NFRs at the start of any design exercise — they will focus your choices and make trade-offs explicit. Closing reflection: which of these concepts do you find easiest to reason about, and which will you practice next?

Here are three concise reminders to keep central: System Design — the process of defining architecture, components, interfaces, and data for requirements. Distributed Systems — systems composed of networked components that require coordination and handling of partial failures. Maintainability — how easily a system can be changed and repaired; this includes code structure, documentation, and automation. Each term ties back to practical choices: you choose components based on NFRs; you manage distributed complexity with clear interfaces; and you reduce long-term cost by investing in maintainability. As a closing reflection, when you next sketch a system, name the primary NFR first and then pick the components that best satisfy it.
